newsitem.title: PERU: Gunmen attack Japanese ambassador's home in Peru.
newsitem.headline: Gunmen attack Japanese ambassador's home in Peru.

text.p: Leftist guerrillas armed with automatic weapons and grenade launchers stormed the Japanese ambassador's residence in Lima on Tuesday and threatened to kill several high-ranking hostages who had been attending a reception to honour the Japanese Emperor's birthday.

Japan's ambassador was captured. Reporters at the scene said other hostages included Peru's Foreign Minister Francisco Tudela, Peru's agriculture minister and the ambassadors of Brazil, Spain and Cuba.
Some of the hostages, including women and elderly, were released, witnesses said.
Japanese Ambassador Morihisa Aoki said in an interview with local radio from within the residency, "For the moment there are no injuries."
The guerrillas threatened to kill their hostages unless authorities released their colleagues from prison, a spokesman for the gunmen told local radio.

"If they do not release our prisoners, we will all die in here," the spokesman said. He said the guerrillas were holding 250 hostages inside the residence, but that could not be confirmed and authorities earlier said they believed 40 hostages were inside the compound.
Witnesses said they heard shots exchanged between the gunmen and police guarding the residence but there were no reports of casualties.
The guerrillas were dressed in black and most of the hostages had their hands held high, according to police on buildings around the embassy.

A guerrilla spokesman from inside the ambassador's residence told a local radio station the attack was carried out by the Cuban-inspired Tupac Amaru Revolutionary Movement (MRTA), the smaller of two communist-guerrilla groups operating in Peru.
The guerrilla spokesman asked for negotiations to begin with government representatives and asked that the talks be broadcast live.
According to reporters at the scene one of the women who was released was the mother of Peruvian President Alberto Fujimori, who is of Japanese descent.
Health Minister Marino Costa Bauer said it was not known who was inside the residence when the attack occurred about 8 p.m. EST (0100 GMT Wednesday).
A Reuter photographer from the roof of a nearby building said he saw about 40 hostages and 20 gunmen armed with rifles and grenade launchers.
Local radio said a number of ambassadors, Peruvian businessmen and academics were at the reception for Japanese Emperor Akihito who turns 63 next Monday.
At the start of the attack at least six explosions were heard, according to police radio reports.
A Japanese diplomat in Lima said he was caught in the attack at the residence and could not leave because of continuing gunfire, a Japanese Foreign Ministry official said in Tokyo.

"I first heard several bombs exploding in front of the official residence of the ambassador," the ministry official quoted Hiroyuki Kimoto, who holds the rank of minister at the embassy, as saying in a call from his mobile telephone.
Peruvian Foreign Minister Francisco Tudela was also among the people taken hostage.
The Japanese Foreign Ministry official said some women were freed by the guerrillas but could not say exactly how many people were inside the compound when the attack occurred.
